title: The HoD Flywheel: Driving Student Progress While Cutting Workload
author: Dominic Salles
summary: Dominic Salles sets out a Head of Department operating model built on one mission, improving the team to improve student progress, while cutting compliance-driven work. The flywheel runs through seven areas: curriculum sequencing with whole-task rehearsal rather than over-scaffolding; spaced retrieval and assessment built around the forgetting curve; collective professional development through shared book looks and question level analysis; controlled teacher experimentation; a repeating 13-week operational rhythm; three non-negotiable classroom techniques (visualiser, cold call, mandatory guessing); and reading whole texts quickly before studying them. He argues that exam mechanics should wait until Year 10, that Tier 2 vocabulary is learned through context while Tier 3 terms are taught explicitly, and that assessment dates should not move to suit data drops. The post ends with a one-page checklist that restates each area as actions.
points: Salles argues the most common curriculum error is making steps too small, so students rehearse components but never the whole task such as a full essay.
He ties assessment to the forgetting curve, separating knowledge tests from application tests and refusing to move test dates for data drops because that destroys spacing.
Professional development is reframed as collaborative: book looks and question level analysis identify the teacher whose approach worked best so it can be written into the scheme of work.
Teachers get one unit a year for a no-penalty experiment, which is his answer to the loss of autonomy in a highly centralised curriculum.
His three classroom non-negotiables are the visualiser, cold call with no volunteers, and mandatory guessing with no blanks.
quotes: The primary mission of any Head of Department (HoD) is simple: Improve the team to improve student progress.
The most common curriculum mistake is making the steps too small, expecting too little effort, and offering vague success models.
Component parts - like thesis statements, embedding quotes, or conclusions - can be rehearsed as separate skills, but they must never replace rehearsing the whole.
Knowledge tests and application tests do not need to happen simultaneously. Knowledge tests must follow the forgetting curve; application tests do not.
Never do book looks or lesson visits alone. Take teachers with you. Conduct book looks together as a department.
Moving it destroys the Ebbinghaus spacing effect and creates false data. It also damages long term memory.

No volunteers. Every student knows they can be selected at random at any moment. This single shift drastically increases attention and the rate of mental retrieval, directly strengthening long-term memory.
You would hate to read books the way you make your students read them! Read first - enjoy, understand, remember the characters and plot. Only then, study it.
